entries.ee39792ce5ef70d873eba710970f0407fdd30f47: <div sID="gen16988" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="62" osisID="Isa.62" sID="Isa.62"/> <div eID="gen16988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16990" type="x-p"/> The business of prophets was both to preach and pray. In this chapter, I. The prophet determines to apply closely and constantly to this business, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. God appoints him and others of his prophets to continue to do so, for the encouragement of his people during the delays of their deliverance, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6-Isa.62.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. III. The promises are here repeated and ratified of the great things God would do for his church, for the Jews after their return out of captivity and for the Christian church when it shall be set up in the world. 1. The church shall be made honourable in the eyes of the world, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. It shall appear to be very dear to God, precious and honourable in his sight, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.3-Isa.62.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 3. It shall enjoy great plenty, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.8-Isa.62.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. 4. It shall be released out of captivity and grow up again into a considerable nation, particularly owned and favoured by heaven, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10-Isa.62.12">ver. 10-12</reference>.
entries.81ecf779f2f1e9cd869b979ce63c4ab1d51fc141: <div eID="gen16990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16989" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prosperity of the Church. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until the righteousness thereof go forth as brightness, and the salvation thereof as a lamp <hi type="italic">that</hi> burneth. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all kings thy glory: and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall name. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzi-bah, and thy land Beulah: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married. <hi type="super">5</hi> For <hi type="italic">as</hi> a young man marrieth a virgin, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall thy sons marry thee: and <hi type="italic">as</hi> the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall thy God rejoice over thee. <div eID="gen16991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16992" type="x-p"/> The prophet here tells us, <div eID="gen16992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16993" type="x-p"/> I. What he will do for the church. A prophet, as he is a seer, so he is a spokesman. This prophet resolves to perform that office faithfully, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">v. 1</reference>. He <hi type="italic">will not hold his peace;</hi> he <hi type="italic">will not rest;</hi> he will mind his business, will take pains, and never desire to take his ease; and herein he was a type of Christ, who was indefatigable in executing the office of a prophet and made it his meat and drink till he had finished his work. Observe here, 1. What the prophet's resolution is: <hi type="italic">He will not hold his peace.</hi> He will continue instant in preaching, will not only faithfully deliver, but frequently repeat, the messages he has <hi type="italic">received from the Lord.</hi> If people receive not the precepts and promises at first, he will inculcate them and give them line upon line. And he will continue instant in prayer; he will never hold his peace at the throne of grace till he has prevailed with God for the mercies promised; he will <hi type="italic">give himself to prayer and to the ministry of the word,</hi> as Christ's ministers must (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.4">Acts vi. 4</reference>), who must labour frequently in both and never be weary of this well-doing. The business of ministers is to speak from God to his people and to God for his people; and in neither of these must they be silent. 2. What is the principle of this resolution—<hi type="italic">for Zion's sake, and for Jerusalem's,</hi> not for the sake of any private interest of his own, but for the church's sake, because he has an affection and concern for Zion, and it lies near his heart. Whatever becomes of his own house and family, he desires to <hi type="italic">see the good of Jerusalem</hi> and resolves to seek it all the days of his life, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.8">Ps. cxxii. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">cxviii. 5</reference>. It is God's Zion and his Jerusalem, and it is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> dear to him, because it is so to God and because God's glory is interested in its prosperity. 3. How long he resolves to continue this importunity—till the promise of the church's righteousness and salvation, given in the foregoing chapter, be accomplished. Isaiah will not himself live to see the release of the captives out of Babylon, much less the bringing in of the gospel, in which <hi type="italic">grace reigns through righteousness unto life</hi> and salvation; yet he will <hi type="italic">not hold his peace till</hi> these be accomplished, even the utmost of them, because his prophecies will continue speaking of these things, and there shall in every age be a remnant that shall continue to pray for them, as successors to him, till the promises be performed, and so the prayers answered that were grounded upon them. Then the church's <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> and <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> will <hi type="italic">go forth as brightness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as a lamp that burns,</hi> so plainly that it will carry its own evidence along with it. It will bring honour and comfort to the church, which will hereupon both look pleasant and appear illustrious; and it will bring instruction and direction to the world, a light not only to the eyes but to the feet, and to <hi type="italic">the paths</hi> of those who before <hi type="italic">sat in darkness and in the shadow of death.</hi> <div eID="gen16993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16994" type="x-p"/> II. What God will do for the church. The prophet can but pray and preach, but God will confirm the word and answer the prayers. 1. The church shall be greatly admired. When that righteousness which is her salvation, her praise, and her glory, shall be <hi type="italic">brought forth,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Gentiles shall see</hi> it. The tidings of it shall be carried to the Gentiles, and a tender of it made to them; they may so see this righteousness as to share in it if it be not their own fault. "Even kings shall see and be in love with the <hi type="italic">glory of thy righteousness</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.2">v. 2</reference>), shall overlook the glory of their own courts and kingdoms, and look at, and look after, the spiritual glory of the church as that which excels. 2. She shall be truly admirable. Great names make men considerable in the world, and great respect is paid them thereupon; now it is agreed that <hi type="italic">honor est in honorante—honour derives its value from the dignity of him who confers it.</hi> God is the fountain of honour and from him the church's honour comes: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be called by a new name,</hi> a pleasant name, such as thou wast never called by before, no, not in the day of thy greatest prosperity, and the reverse of that which thou wast called by in the day of thy affliction; thou shalt have a new character, be advanced to a new dignity, and those about thee shall have new thoughts of thee." This seems to be alluded to in that promise (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.17">Rev. ii. 17</reference>) of the <hi type="italic">white stone and in the stone a new name,</hi> and that (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Rev. iii. 12</reference>) of the <hi type="italic">name of the city of my God</hi> and my <hi type="italic">new name.</hi> It is a name <hi type="italic">which the mouth of the Lord shall name,</hi> who, we are sure, miscalls nothing, and who will oblige others to call her by the name he has given her; for his judgment is according to truth and all shall concur with it sooner or later. Two names God shall give her:—(1.) He shall call her his crown (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord,</hi> not on his head (as adding any real honour or power to him, as crowns do to those that are crowned with them), but in his hand. He is pleased to account them, and show them forth, as a glory and beauty to him. When he took them to be his people it was that they might be <hi type="italic">unto him for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>): "Thou shalt be a <hi type="italic">crown of glory</hi> and a <hi type="italic">royal diadem,</hi> through the hand, the good hand, of thy God upon thee; he shall make thee so, for he shall be <hi type="italic">to thee a crown of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">ch. xxviii. 5</reference>. Thou shalt be so <hi type="italic">in his hand,</hi> that is, under his protection; he that shall put glory upon thee shall <hi type="italic">create a defence upon all that glory,</hi> so that the flowers of thy crown shall never wither nor shall its jewels be lost." (2.) He shall call her his spouse, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.4-Isa.62.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. This is a yet greater honour, especially considering what a forlorn condition she had been in. [1.] Her case had been very melancholy. She was called <hi type="italic">forsaken</hi> and her land <hi type="italic">desolate</hi> during the captivity, like a woman reproachfully divorced or left a disconsolate widow. Such as the state of religion in the world before the preaching of the gospel—it was in a manner forsaken and desolate, a thing that no man looked after nor had any real concern for. [2.] It should now be very pleasant, for God would return in mercy to her. Instead of those two names of reproach, she shall be called by two honourable names. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She shall be called <hi type="italic">Hephzi-bah,</hi> which signifies, <hi type="italic">My delight is in her;</hi> it was the name of Hezekiah's queen, Manasseh's mother (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.1">2 Kings xxi. 1</reference>), a proper name for a wife, who ought to be her husband's delight, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Prov. v. 19</reference>. And here it is the church's Maker that is her husband: <hi type="italic">The Lord delights in thee.</hi> God by his grace has wrought that in his church which makes her his delight, she being refined, and reformed, and brought home to him; and then by his providence he does that for her which makes it appear that she is his delight and that he delights to do her good. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She shall be called <hi type="italic">Beulah,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">married,</hi> whereas she had been desolate, a condition opposed to that of the <hi type="italic">married wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">ch. liv. 1</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thy land shall be married,</hi> that is, it shall become fruitful again, and be replenished." Though she has long been barren, she shall again be peopled, shall again be made to keep house and to be a joyful mother of children, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.9">Ps. cxiii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">She shall be married,</hi> for, 1. Her sons shall heartily espouse the land of their nativity and its interests, which they had for a long time neglected, as despairing ever to have any comfortable enjoyment of it: <hi type="italic">Thy sons shall marry thee,</hi> that is, they shall live with thee and take delight in thee. When they were in Babylon, they seemed to have espoused that land, for they were appointed to settle, and to seek the peace of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.5-Jer.29.7">Jer. xxix. 5-7</reference>. But now they shall again marry their own land, <hi type="italic">as a young man marries a virgin</hi> that he takes great delight in, is extremely fond of, and is likely to have many children by. It bodes well to a land when its own natives and inhabitants are pleased with it, prefer it before other lands, when its princes marry their country and resolve to take their lot with it. 2. <hi type="italic">Her God</hi> (which is much better) shall <hi type="italic">betroth her to himself in righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.19-Hos.2.20">Hosea ii. 19, 20</reference>. He will take pleasure in his church: <hi type="italic">As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride,</hi> is pleased with his relation to her and her affection to him, <hi type="italic">so shall thy God rejoice over thee:</hi> he shall rest in his love to thee (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zeph. iii. 17</reference>); <hi type="italic">he shall take pleasure</hi> in thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Ps. cxlvii. 11</reference>), and shall <hi type="italic">delight to do thee good with his whole heart and his whole soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">Jer. xxxii. 41</reference>. This is very applicable to the love Christ has for his church and the complacency he takes in it, which appears so brightly in Solomon's Song, and which will be complete in heaven.
entries.c119f0075718b250e36924c3348b5f361bab0aa5: <div eID="gen16994" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prosperity of the Church. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , keep not silence, <hi type="super">7</hi> And give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength, Surely I will no more give thy corn <hi type="italic">to be</hi> meat for thine enemies; and the sons of the stranger shall not drink thy wine, for the which thou hast laboured: <hi type="super">9</hi> But they that have gathered it shall eat it, and praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and they that have brought it together shall drink it in the courts of my holiness. <div eID="gen16995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16996" type="x-p"/> Two things are here promised to Jerusalem:— <div eID="gen16996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> I. Plenty of the means of grace—abundance of good preaching and good praying (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6-Isa.62.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), and this shows the method God takes when he designs mercy for a people; he first brings them to their duty and pours out a spirit of prayer upon them, and then brings salvation to them. Provision is made, <div eID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> 1. That ministers may do their duty as watchmen. It is here spoken of as a token for good, as a step towards further mercy and an earnest of it, that, in order to what he designed for them, he would set <hi type="italic">watchmen on their walls who should never hold their peace.</hi> Note, (1.) Ministers are watchmen on the church's walls, for it is as a city besieged, whose concern it is to have sentinels on the walls, to take notice and give notice of the motions of the enemy. It is necessary that, as watchmen, they be wakeful, and faithful, and willing to endure hardness. (2.) They are concerned to stand upon their guard day and night; they must never be off their watch as long as those for whose souls they watch are not out of danger. (3.) They must never hold their peace; they must take all opportunities to give warning to sinners, in season, out of season, and must never betray the cause of Christ by a treacherous or cowardly silence. They must never hold their peace at the throne of grace; they must <hi type="italic">pray, and not faint,</hi> as Moses lifted up his hands and kept them steady, till Israel had obtained the victory over Amalek, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.10">Exod. xvii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16999" type="x-p"/> 2. That people may do their duty. As those that make mention of the Lord, let not them keep silence neither, let not them think it enough that their watchmen pray for them, but let them pray for themselves; all will be little enough to meet the approaching mercy with due solemnity. Note, (1.) It is the character of God's professing people that they make mention of the Lord, and continue to do so even in bad times, when the land is termed <hi type="italic">forsaken</hi> and <hi type="italic">desolate.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">the Lord's remembrancers</hi> (so the margin reads it); they remember the Lord themselves and put one another in mind of him. (2.) God's professing people must be a praying people, must be public-spirited in prayer, must wrestle with God in prayer, and continue to do so: "<hi type="italic">Keep not silence;</hi> never grow remiss in the duty nor weary of it." <hi type="italic">Give him no rest</hi>—alluding to an importunate beggar, to the widow that with her continual coming wearied the judge into a compliance. God said to <hi type="italic">Moses, Let me alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Exod. xxxii. 10</reference>), and Jacob to Christ, <hi type="italic">I will not let thee go except thou bless me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Gen. xxxii. 26</reference>. (3.) God is so far from being displeased with our pressing importunity, as men commonly are, that he invites and encourages it; he bids us to cry after him; he is not like those disciples who discouraged a petitioner, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">Matt. xv. 23</reference>. He bids us make pressing applications at the throne of grace, and <hi type="italic">give him no rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.5">Luke xi. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.8">8</reference>. He suffers himself not only to be reasoned with, but to be wrestled with. (4.) The public welfare or prosperity of God's Jerusalem is that which we should be most importunate for at the throne of grace; we should pray for the good of the church. [1.] That it may be safe, that he would <hi type="italic">establish</hi> it, that the interests of the church may be firm, may be settled for the present and secured to posterity. [2.] That it may be great, may be <hi type="italic">a praise in the earth,</hi> that it may be praised, and God may be praised for it. When gospel truths are cleared and vindicated, when gospel ordinances are duly administered in their purity and power, when the church becomes eminent for holiness and love, then Jerusalem is a praise in the earth, then it is in reputation. (5.) We must persevere in our prayers for mercy to the church till the mercy come; we must do as the prophet's servant did, go yet seven times, till the promising cloud appear, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1 Kings xviii. 44</reference>. (6.) It is a good sign that God is coming towards a people in ways of mercy when he pours out a spirit of prayer upon them and stirs them up to be fervent and constant in their intercessions. <div eID="gen16999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17000" type="x-p"/> II. Plenty of all other good things, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.8">v. 8</reference>. This follows upon the former; when the people praise God, when <hi type="italic">all the people praise him, then shall the earth yield her increase</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.5-Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 5, 6</reference>), and outward prosperity, crowning its piety, shall help to make Jerusalem a praise in the earth. Observe, <div eID="gen17000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17001" type="x-p"/> 1. The great distress they had been in, and the losses they had sustained. Their corn had been meat for their enemies, which they hoped would be meat for themselves and their families. Here was a double grievance, that they themselves wanted that which was necessary to the support of life and were in danger of perishing for want of it, and that their enemies were strengthened by it, had their camp victualled with it, and so were the better able to do them a mischief. God is said to give their corn to their enemies, because he not only permitted it, but ordered it, to be the just punishment both of their abuse of plenty and of their symbolizing with strangers, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7">ch. i. 7</reference>. The wine which they had laboured for, and which in their affliction they needed for the relief of those among them that were of a heavy heart, strangers drank it, to gratify their lusts with; this sore judgment was threatened for their sins, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev. xxvi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">Deut. xxviii. 33</reference>. See how uncertain our creature-comforts are, and how much it is our wisdom to labour for that meat which we can never be robbed of. <div eID="gen17001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17002" type="x-p"/> 2. The great fulness and satisfaction they should now be restored to (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that have gathered it shall eat it, and praise the Lord.</hi> See here, (1.) God's mercy in giving plenty, and peace to enjoy it,—that the earth yields her increase, that there are hands to be employed in gathering it in, and that they are not taken off by plague and sickness, or otherwise employed in war,—that strangers and enemies do not come and gather it for themselves, or take it from us when we have gathered it,—that we eat the labour of our hands and the bread is not eaten out of our mouths,—and especially that we have opportunity and a heart to honour God with it, and that his courts are open to us and we are not restrained from attending on him in them. (2.) Our duty in the enjoyment of this mercy. We must gather what God gives, with care and industry; we must eat it freely and cheerfully, not bury the gifts of God's bounty, but make use of them. We must, when we have eaten and are full, <hi type="italic">bless the Lord,</hi> and give him thanks for his bounty to us; and we must serve him with our abundance, use it in works of piety and charity, eat it and <hi type="italic">drink it in the courts of his holiness,</hi> where the altar, the priest, and the poor must all have their share. The greatest comfort that a good man has in his meat and drink is that it furnishes him with a meat-offering and a drink-offering for the Lord his God (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.14">Joel ii. 14</reference>); the greatest comfort that he has in an estate is that it gives him an opportunity of honouring God and doing good. This wine is to be <hi type="italic">drunk in the courts of God's holiness,</hi> and therefore moderately and with sobriety, as before the Lord. <div eID="gen17002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17003" type="x-p"/> 3. The solemn ratification of this promise: <hi type="italic">The Lord has sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength,</hi> that he will do this for his people. God confirms it by an oath, that his people, who trust in him and his word, may have <hi type="italic">strong consolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. And, since he can swear by no greater, he swears by himself, sometimes by his being (<hi type="italic">As I live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.11">Ezek. xxxiii. 11</reference>), sometimes by his holiness (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>), here by his power, his right hand (which was lifted up in swearing, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.40">Deut. xxxii. 40</reference>), and his arm of power; for it is a great satisfaction to those who build their hopes on God's promise to be sure that <hi type="italic">what he has promised he is able to perform,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.21">Rom. iv. 21</reference>. To assure us of this he has sworn by his strength, pawning the reputation of his omnipotence upon it; if he do not do it, let it be said, <hi type="italic">It was because he could not,</hi> which the Egyptians shall never say (<reference osisRef="Num.14.16">Num. xiv. 16</reference>) nor any other. It is the comfort of God's people that his power is engaged for them, his right hand, where the Mediator sits.
entries.039d29498b0ffa2a1de4e7c1fcc6dc7b4c8bbbc9: <div eID="gen17003" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advent of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen17004" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Go through, go through the gates; prepare ye the way of the people; cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones; lift up a standard for the people. <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath proclaimed unto the end of the world, Say ye to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh; behold, his reward <hi type="italic">is</hi> with him, and his work before him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they shall call them, The holy people, The redeemed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken. <div eID="gen17004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17005" type="x-p"/> This, as many like passages before, refers to the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon, and, under the type and figure of that, to the great redemption wrought out by Jesus Christ, and the proclaiming of gospel grace and liberty through him. 1. Way shall be made for this salvation; all difficulties shall be removed, and whatever might obstruct it shall be taken out of the way, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">v. 10</reference>. The gates of Babylon shall be thrown open, that they may with freedom go through them; the way from Babylon to the land of Israel shall be prepared; causeways shall be made and cast up through wet and miry places, and the stones gathered out from places rough and rocky; in the convenient places appointed for their rendezvous standards shall be set up for their direction and encouragement, that they may embody for their greater safety. Thus John Baptist was sent to <hi type="italic">prepare the way of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.3.3">Matt. iii. 3</reference>. And, before Christ by his graces and comforts comes to any for salvation, preparation is made for him by repentance, which is called the <hi type="italic">preparation of the gospel of peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.15">Eph. vi. 15</reference>. Here the way is levelled by it, there the feet are shod with it, which comes all to one, for both are in order to a journey. 2. Notice shall be given of this salvation, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.11-Isa.62.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. It shall be proclaimed to the captives that they are set at liberty and may go if they please; it shall be proclaimed to their neighbours, to all about them, <hi type="italic">to the end of the world,</hi> that God has pleaded Zion's just, injured, and despised cause. Let is be said to Zion, for her comfort, <hi type="italic">Behold, thy salvation comes</hi> (that is, thy Saviour, who brings salvation); he will bring such a work, such a reward, in this salvation, as shall be admired by all, a reward of comfort and peace with him; but a work of humiliation and reformation before him, to prepare his people for that recompence of their sufferings; and then, with reference to each, it follows, they shall be called, <hi type="italic">The holy people,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">redeemed of the Lord. The work before him,</hi> which shall be wrought in them and upon them, shall denominate them a holy people, cured of their inclination to idolatry and consecrated to God only; and the <hi type="italic">reward with him,</hi> the deliverance wrought for them, shall denominate them the <hi type="italic">redeemed of the Lord,</hi> so redeemed as none but God could redeem them, and redeemed to be his, their bonds loosed, that they might be his servants. Jerusalem shall then be called, <hi type="italic">Sought out, a city not forsaken.</hi> She had been forsaken for many years; there were neither traders nor worshippers that enquired the way to Jerusalem as formerly, when it was frequented by both. But now God will again make her considerable. She shall be sought out, visited, resorted to, and court made to her, as much as ever. When Jerusalem is called a <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> then it is called <hi type="italic">sought out;</hi> for holiness puts an honour and beauty upon any place or person, which draws respect, and makes them to be admired, beloved, and enquired after. But this being proclaimed to the end of the world must have a reference to the gospel of Christ, which was to be preached to every creature; and it intimates, (1.) The glory of Christ. It is published immediately to the church, but is thence echoed to every nation: <hi type="italic">Behold, thy salvation cometh.</hi> Christ is not only the Saviour, but the salvation itself; for the happiness of believers is not only from him, but in him, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">ch. xii. 2</reference>. His salvation consists both in the work and in the reward which he brings with him; for those that are his shall neither be idle nor lose their labour. (2.) The beauty of the church. Christians shall be called <hi type="italic">saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1 Cor. i. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the holy people,</hi> for they are chosen and called <hi type="italic">to salvation through sanctification.</hi> They shall be called <hi type="italic">the redeemed of the Lord;</hi> to him they owe their liberty, and therefore to him they owe their service, and they shall not be ashamed to own both. None are to be <hi type="italic">called the redeemed of the Lord</hi> but those that are the <hi type="italic">holy people;</hi> the people of God's purchase are a holy nation. And they shall be called, <hi type="italic">Sought out.</hi> God shall seek them out, and find them, wherever they are dispersed, eclipsed, or lost in a crowd; men shall seek them out, that they may join themselves to them, and not forsake them. It is good to associate with <hi type="italic">the holy people,</hi> that we may learn their ways, and with <hi type="italic">the redeemed of the Lord,</hi> that we may share in the blessings of the redemption.  <chapter eID="Isa.62"/> <div eID="gen17005" type="x-p"/>

entries.023d3de4575d10500d5036d2b83524022687fd8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9481"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 62</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.62.1-Isa.62.12">Is 62:1-12</reference>. Intercessory Prayers for Zion's Restoration, Accompanying God's Promises of It, as the Appointed Means of Accomplishing It.</title> <div sID="gen16523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9481"/><hi type="bold">1. I--</hi>the prophet, as representative of all the praying people of God who love and intercede for Zion (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.17">Psa 102:13-17</reference>), or else Messiah (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>). So Messiah is represented as unfainting in His efforts for His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Is 42:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">50:7</reference>).<div eID="gen16523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness thereof--</hi>not its own inherently, but imputed to it, for its restoration to God's favor: hence "salvation" answers to it in the parallelism. "Judah" is to be "saved" through "the Lord our (Judah's and the Church's) righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as brightness--</hi>properly the bright shining of the rising sun (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Is 60:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen16525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lamp--</hi>blazing torch. <div eID="gen16526" type="x-p"/>
entries.989aea11a9337ef8237cc9e3409448d40bfeecc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9482"/><div sID="gen16527" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9482"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Is 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1-Isa.42.6">42:1-6</reference>; 49:7, 22, 23; 60:3, 5, 16).<div eID="gen16527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new name--</hi>expression of thy new and improved condition (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">Is 62:4</reference>), the more valuable and lasting as being conferred by Jehovah Himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.12">Is 62:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.15">Is 65:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.17">Re 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen16528" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4b57074066a87f741ddac61b52ea026e69b901d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9483"/><div sID="gen16529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9483"/>3. (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.16">Zec 9:16</reference>)<div eID="gen16529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... hand of ... Lord--</hi>As a crown is worn on the head, not "in the hand," hand must here be figurative for "under the Lord's protection" (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">De 33:3</reference>). "All His saints are in thy hand." His people are in His hand at the same time that they are "a crown of glory" to Him (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Re 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">19:12</reference>); reciprocally, He is "a crown of glory and a diadem of beauty" to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">Is 28:5</reference>; compare Mal 3:17). <div eID="gen16530" type="x-p"/>
entries.725051472e8cc748e1c92dc854350c8bd0115fe9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9484"/><div sID="gen16531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9484"/><hi type="bold">4. be termed--</hi>be "forsaken," so as that that term could be applicable to thee.<div eID="gen16531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hephzi-bah--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.1">2Ki 21:1</reference>), the name of Hezekiah's wife, a type of Jerusalem, as Hezekiah was of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>): "my delight is in her."<div eID="gen16532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beulah--</hi>"Thou art married." See the same contrast of Zion's past and future state under the same figure (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.4-Isa.54.6">Is 54:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen16533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land ... married--</hi>to Jehovah as its Lord and Husband: implying not only ownership, but protection on the part of the Owner [Horsley]. <div eID="gen16534" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1596b4957b445d88a350e8c77acdf59e8ecf6aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9485"/><div sID="gen16535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9485"/><hi type="bold">5. thy sons--</hi>rather, changing the points, which are of no authority in Hebrew, "thy builder" or "restorer," that is, God; for in the parallel clause, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">Is 62:4</reference>, God is implied as being "married" to her; whereas her "sons" could hardly be said to marry their mother; and in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.18">Is 49:18</reference>, they are said to be her bridal ornaments, not her husband. The plural form, builders, is used of God in reverence as "husbands" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over the bride--</hi>in the possession of the bride (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.19">Is 65:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">Jr 32:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen16536" type="x-p"/>
entries.6150a595e21033c55d3d766dc55bc45f4f639007: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9486"/><div sID="gen16537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9486"/><hi type="bold">6. I--</hi>Isaiah speaking in the person of the Messiah.<div eID="gen16537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watchmen upon ... walls--</hi>image from the watches set upon a city's wall to look out for the approach of a messenger with good tidings (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">8</reference>); the good tidings of the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon, prefiguring the return from the present dispersion (compare Is 21:6-11; 56:<reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.7">33:7</reference>). The watches in the East are announced by a loud cry to mark the vigilance of the watchmen.<div eID="gen16538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye that ... mention ... Lord--</hi>Hebrew, "ye that are the Lord's remembrancers"; God's servants who by their prayers "put God in remembrance" of His promises (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Is 43:26</reference>); we are required to remind God, as if God could, which He cannot, forget His promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.49">Psa 119:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jr 14:21</reference>). <div eID="gen16539" type="x-p"/>
entries.a885dca81b8630264bebde8b51ae033814cbbf15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9487"/><div sID="gen16540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9487"/><hi type="bold">7. no rest--</hi>Hebrew, "silence"; keep not silence yourselves, nor let Him rest in silence. Compare as to Messiah Himself, "I will not hold ... peace ... not rest" (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">Is 62:1</reference>); Messiah's watchmen (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>) imitate Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">Is 62:1</reference>) in intercessory "prayer without ceasing" for Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.6">Psa 122:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">51:18</reference>); also for the spiritual Jerusalem, the Church (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.1">Lu 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Ro 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen16540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a praise--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">Is 61:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.20">Zep 3:20</reference>). <div eID="gen16541" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4d3248f00ca869f6bdfad43e28456fa7a04b69c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9488"/><div sID="gen16542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9488"/><hi type="bold">8. sworn by ... right hand--</hi>His mighty instrument of accomplishing His will (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Is 45:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.13">He 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons of ... stranger--</hi>Foreigners shall no more rob thee of the fruit of thy labors (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.65.21">Is 65:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen16543" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbfad4604c90eaf453395434788e024c3178bb7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9489"/><div sID="gen16544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9489"/><hi type="bold">9. eat ... and praise--</hi>not consume it on their own lusts, and without thanksgiving.<div eID="gen16544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink it in ... courts--</hi>They who have gathered the vintage shall drink it at the feasts held in the courts surrounding the temple (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">De 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.23">14:23</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen16545" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe925a05b76340a2f48212889434a6ee40983f7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9490"/><div sID="gen16546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9490"/>10. What Isaiah in the person of Messiah had engaged in (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">Is 62:1</reference>) unrestingly to seek, and what the watchmen were unrestingly to pray for (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">Is 62:7</reference>), and what Jehovah solemnly promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.8">Is 62:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.9">9</reference>), is now to be fulfilled; the Gentile nations are commanded to "go through the gates" (either of their own cities [Rosenmuller] or of Jerusalem [Maurer]), in order to remove all obstacles out of "the way of the people (Israel)" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Is 40:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10-Isa.52.12">52:10-12</reference>).<div eID="gen16546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">standard--</hi>for the dispersed Jews to rally round, with a view to their return (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Is 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">11:12</reference>). <div eID="gen16547" type="x-p"/>
entries.271a4fd17f5c91c98fc1c0254cc5aa5e85254ab2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9491"/><div sID="gen16548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9491"/><hi type="bold">11. salvation--</hi>embodied in the Saviour (see <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his work--</hi>rather, recompense (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Is 40:10</reference>). <div eID="gen16549" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7559b9a55886de9e2c67ed341499a578b8448df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9492"/><div sID="gen16550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9492"/><hi type="bold">12. Sought out--</hi>Sought after and highly prized by Jehovah; answering to "not forsaken" in the parallel clause; no longer abandoned, but loved; image from a wife (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">Is 62:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.14">Jr 30:14</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.62"/>

entries.2a6a612f259c93faaa3e2e84a8de11eeb4b4054e: <div eID="gen28930" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28931" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28932" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28932" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28931" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28933" type="x-p"/> The prophet opens this chapter with ardent prayers that the happy period of reconciliation just now promised, and here again foretold, may be hastened, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.1-Isa.62.5">Isa 62:1-5</reference>. He then calls upon the faithful, particularly the priests and Levites, to join him, urging the promises, and even the oath, of Jehovah, as the foundation of their request, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6-Isa.62.9">Isa 62:6-9</reference>. And, relying on this oath, he goes on to speak of the general restoration promised, as already performing; and calls to the people to march forth, and to the various nations among whom they are dispersed to prepare the way for them, as God had caused the order for their return to be universally proclaimed, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10-Isa.62.12">Isa 62:10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen28933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28934" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28935" type="x-p"/> For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace - These are the words of Jehovah declaring his purpose relative to the events predicted in the preceding chapter. <div eID="gen28935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28936" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be called by a new name - Viz., Christian - or, as in the fourth verse, חפצי בה chephtsi bah, "my delight is in her" - because she has now received that command, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; Hear Him."
entries.2bca812e448cc37d8b2e7cfd2915fb13f715c1d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28937" type="x-p"/> Thy land Beulah - בעולה beulah, married. In the prophets, a desolate land is represented under the notion of a widow; an inhabited land, under that of a married woman, who has both a husband and children.
entries.8f783fc026cb125e7a032602f0281848508e46e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen28937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28938" type="x-p"/> For as a young man - so - The particles of comparison are not at present in the Hebrew Text: but the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee seem to have read in their copies כ caph prefixed to the verb, כי כיבעל ki keyibal which seems to have been omitted by mistake of a transcriber, occasioned by the repetition of the same two letters. And before the verb in the second line a MS. adds כן ken, so; which the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee seem also to have had in their copies. In the third line of this verse the same MS. has in like manner וכמשוש vechimsos, and two MSS. and the Babylonish Talmud כמשוש kimsos, adding the כ caph; and in the fourth line, the Babylonish Talmud likewise adds כן ken, so, before the verb. <div eID="gen28938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28939" type="x-p"/> Sir John Chardin, in his note on this place, tells us, "that it is the custom in the east for youths, that were never married, always to marry virgins; and widowers, however young, to marry widows." - Harmer, Observ. 2 p. 482. <div eID="gen28939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28940" type="x-p"/> So shall thy sons marry thee - For בניך banayich, thy sons, Bishop Lowth reads, restorer or builder, as he does not consider the word as the plural of בן ben, a son, but the participle benoni of the verb בנה banah, he built. I do not see that we gain much by this translation. Thy sons shall dwell in thee, Vulgate; and so the Septuagint and Chaldee.
entries.21fdfe0de1afe9eb484b2f72b374dd08a449f848: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28941" type="x-p"/> Ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence - The faithful, and in particular the priests and Levites, are exhorted by the prophet to beseech God with unremitted importunity (compare <reference osisRef="Luk.18.1">Luk 18:1</reference>, etc.) to hasten the redemption of Sion. The image in this place is taken from the temple service; in which there was appointed a constant watch, day and night, by the Levites: and among them this seems to have belonged particularly to the singers, see <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">1Chr 9:33</reference>. Now the watches in the east, even to this day, are performed by a loud cry from time to time of the watchmen, to mark the time, and that very frequently, and in order to show that they themselves are constantly attentive to their duty. Hence the watchmen are said by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>, to lift up their voice; and here they are commanded, not to keep silence; and the greatest reproach to them is, that they are dumb dogs; they cannot bark; dreamers; sluggards, loving to slumber, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Isa 56:10</reference>. "The watchmen in the camp of the caravans go their rounds crying one after another, 'God is one, he is merciful:' and often add, 'Take heed to yourselves.'" Tavernier, Voyage de Perse, 54:1 chap. 10. The hundred and thirty-fourth Psalm gives us an example of the temple watch. The whole Psalm is nothing more than the alternate cry of two different divisions of the watch. The first watch addresses the second, reminding them of their duty; the second answers by a solemn blessing. The address and the answer seem both to be a set form, which each division proclaimed, or sung aloud, at stated intervals, to notify the time of the night: - <div eID="gen28941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28942" type="x-p"/> First Chorus "Come on now, bless ye Jehovah, all ye servants of Jehovah; <div eID="gen28942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28943" type="x-p"/> Ye that stand in the house of Jehovah in the nights; <div eID="gen28943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28944" type="x-p"/> Lift up your hands towards the sanctuary, <div eID="gen28944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28945" type="x-p"/> And bless ye Jehovah." <div eID="gen28945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28946" type="x-p"/> Second Chorus "Jehovah bless thee out of Sion; <div eID="gen28946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28947" type="x-p"/> He that made heaven and earth." "Ye who stand in the place of the watch, in the house of the sanctuary of the Lord; and ye praise through the nights;" - says the Chaldee paraphrase on the second line. And this explains what is here particularly meant by proclaiming, or making remembrance of, the name of Jehovah: the form, which the watch made use of on these occasions, was always a short sentence, expressing some pious sentiment, of which Jehovah was the subject; and it is remarkable, that the custom in the east in this respect also still continues the very same; as appears by the example above given from Tavernier. <div eID="gen28947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28948" type="x-p"/> And this observation leads to the explanation of an obscure passage in the Prophet Malachi, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.12">Mal 2:12</reference>. "Jehovah will cut off the man that doeth this; <div eID="gen28948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28949" type="x-p"/> The watchman and the answerer, from the tabernacles of Jacob; <div eID="gen28949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28950" type="x-p"/> And him that presenteth an offering to Jehovah God of hosts." ער וענה er veoneh, the master and the scholar, says our translation, after the Vulgate: the son and the grandson, says the Syriac and Chaldee, as little to the purpose: Arias Montanus has given it vigilantem et respondentem, "the watchman and the answerer;" that is, the Levite and "him that presenteth an offering to Jehovah," that is, the priest. - L. Ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence. Is not this clause an address to the ministers of Christ, to continue in supplication for the conversion of the Jewish people? Kimchi seems to think that the watchmen are the interceding angels!
entries.2855ba36f6f7a286e3f50b151424731ef918e551: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28951" type="x-p"/> But they that have gathered it shall eat it, and praise the Lord - This and the following line have reference to the law of Moses: "Thou mayest not eat within thy gates the tithe of thy corn, or of thy wine, or of thy oil; but thou must eat them before the Lord thy God, in the place which the Lord thy God shall choose," <reference osisRef="Deu.12.17">Deu 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.12.18">Deu 12:18</reference>. "And when ye shall come into the land, and shall have planted all manner of trees for food, then ye shall count the fruit thereof as uncircumcised: three years it shall be as uncircumcised unto you; it shall not be eaten of. But in the fourth year all the fruit thereof shall be holy to praise the Lord withal. And in the fifth year ye shall eat the fruit thereof," <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">Lev 19:23-25</reference>. This clearly explains the force of the expressions, "shall praise Jehovah," and "shall drink it in my sacred courts." <div eID="gen28951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28952" type="x-p"/> Five MSS., one ancient, have יאכלוהו yocheluhu, they shall eat it, fully expressed: and so likewise ישתוהו yishtuhu, they shall drink it, is found in nineteen MSS., three of them ancient. - L.
entries.71e3309d28e5fa9f306e9e47f0bea8d67b6862e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28953" type="x-p"/> Of the people "For the people" - Before the word העם haam, the people, two MSS. insert יהוה Yehovah; one MS. adds the same word after; and eight MSS., three ancient, instead of העם haam, have יהוה Yehovah, and so likewise one edition. But though it makes a good sense either way, I believe it to be an interpolation, as the ancient Versions do not favor it. The Septuagint indeed read עמי ammi, my people. - L.
entries.ef2e61e1bb5e9e9aacac22e0db9ee6b59bac8ed0: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28954" type="x-p"/> Unto the end of the world - אל קצה הארץ el ketseh haarets - Instead of אל el, to, עד ad, Unto, is the reading of two of Kennicott's MSS.; and one of mine has מקצה mikketseh, "From the end of the earth." <div eID="gen28954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28955" type="x-p"/> Behold, thy salvation cometh "Lo, thy Savior cometh" - So all the ancient Versions render the word ישעך yishech. <div eID="gen28955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28956" type="x-p"/> Behold, his reward - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Isa 40:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa 40:11</reference>. This reward he carries as it were in his hand. His work is before him - he perfectly knows what is to be done; and is perfectly able to do it. He will do what God should do, and what man cannot do; and men should be workers with him. Let no man fear that the promise shall not be fulfilled on account of its difficulty, its greatness, the hinderances in the way, or the unworthiness of the person to whom it is made. It is God's work; he is able to do it, and as willing as he is able.
